title: PHY 103 — General Physics III: Behaviour of Matter
topic: Elasticity and Properties of Solids & States of Matter and Fluid Behavior
overview: This study pack covers the mechanical properties of matter, including elasticity, states of matter, and fluid behavior — foundational concepts for later materials and fluid mechanics courses.

modules.title: Elasticity and Properties of Solids
modules.summary:
When a force is applied to a solid material, it deforms. If the material returns to its original shape once the force is removed, the deformation is elastic; if it doesn't, the deformation is plastic. Hooke's Law describes elastic behavior: the extension of a material is directly proportional to the applied force, within the elastic limit.

Hooke's Law is expressed as F = kx, where F is the applied force, k is the spring constant (stiffness), and x is the extension. Beyond the elastic limit, a material undergoes permanent deformation and no longer obeys Hooke's Law.

This behavior directly connects to later Strength of Materials coursework, where stress-strain relationships are explored in more depth.
keyPoints: Elastic deformation: material returns to original shape after force is removed
Plastic deformation: permanent shape change remains after force is removed
Hooke's Law: F = kx (force equals spring constant times extension)
The elastic limit is the point beyond which Hooke's Law no longer applies
The spring constant (k) measures a material's stiffness — higher k means stiffer material

definitions.definition: The principle that the extension of an elastic material is directly proportional to the applied force, within the elastic limit (F = kx).
A measure of a material's stiffness, representing the force needed to produce a unit extension.
The maximum force or stress a material can withstand while still returning to its original shape.
Permanent deformation of a material that remains after the applied force is removed.

workedExamples.title: Applying Hooke's Law
workedExamples.problem: A spring with a spring constant of 200 N/m is stretched by 0.05 m. Find the force applied.

workedExamples.title: Finding Extension from Force
workedExamples.problem: A force of 15 N is applied to a spring with a spring constant of 300 N/m. Find the extension.

quiz.question: What does Hooke's Law state?
options: Extension is directly proportional to applied force, within the elastic limit
Energy cannot be created or destroyed
Pressure equals force divided by area
quiz.explanation: Hooke's Law (F = kx) states that extension is proportional to applied force, as long as the material remains within its elastic limit.

quiz.question: What happens to a material once it passes its elastic limit?
options: It returns to its original shape
quiz.explanation: Beyond the elastic limit, a material no longer returns to its original shape — it undergoes permanent plastic deformation.

modules.title: States of Matter and Fluid Behavior
modules.summary:
Matter exists primarily in three states — solid, liquid, and gas — distinguished by the arrangement and movement of their particles. Solids have fixed shape and volume; liquids have fixed volume but take the shape of their container; gases have neither fixed shape nor volume.

Pressure in fluids is defined as force per unit area (P = F/A), and in a static fluid, pressure increases with depth according to P = ρgh, where ρ is fluid density, g is gravitational acceleration, and h is depth.

Pascal's Principle states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions — this is the working principle behind hydraulic systems, directly relevant to engineering applications like hydraulic brakes and lifts.
keyPoints: Three states of matter: solid (fixed shape/volume), liquid (fixed volume, variable shape), gas (neither fixed)
Pressure: P = F/A (force per unit area)
Pressure in a static fluid: P = ρgh (density × gravity × depth)
Pascal's Principle: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid transmits equally in all directions
Pascal's Principle is the basis for hydraulic systems like car brakes and lifts

definitions.definition: Force applied per unit area, calculated as P = F/A, measured in Pascals (Pa).
The mass of a fluid per unit volume, a key factor in determining pressure at depth.
The principle that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally throughout the fluid in all directions.
A system that uses fluid pressure, based on Pascal's Principle, to transmit force and do mechanical work.

workedExamples.title: Calculating Pressure at Depth
workedExamples.problem: Find the pressure at a depth of 10 m in water (density = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s²).
workedExamples.answer: The pressure at 10 m depth is 98,000 Pa (98 kPa).

workedExamples.title: Applying Pascal's Principle to a Hydraulic Lift
workedExamples.problem: A hydraulic lift has a small piston of area 0.01 m² and a large piston of area 0.5 m². If a force of 50 N is applied to the small piston, find the force generated on the large piston.
steps: Apply Pascal's Principle: pressure is equal throughout the fluid, so P1 = P2
Since P2 = P1, F2 = P2 × A2 = 5000 Pa × 0.5 m²
workedExamples.answer: The large piston generates a force of 2500 N — a 50x amplification, illustrating how hydraulic systems multiply force.

quiz.question: What is the formula for pressure in a static fluid at depth h?
quiz.explanation: Pressure at depth in a static fluid is calculated as P = ρgh (density × gravitational acceleration × depth).

quiz.question: What does Pascal's Principle state?
options: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions
quiz.explanation: Pascal's Principle explains that pressure in an enclosed fluid is distributed equally in every direction, enabling hydraulic force multiplication.
